At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-994)
response:
Mechanistic interpretability research has established that transformer neurons vary along a spectrum from monosemantic (activating for a single, coherent concept) to polysemantic (activating for multiple unrelated concepts via superposition). The central question here is whether pruning — removing weights or neurons to compress a model — differentially destroys features depending on which type of neuron encodes them. The working hypothesis is an asymmetry: polysemantic neurons may appear expendable by standard importance metrics (their per-feature activation signal is diluted across concepts), while monosemantic neurons, being more interpretable and "clean," may ironically be pruned more aggressively because their narrow tuning makes them look like low-utility specialists rather than broad contributors. What a beginner misses is that standard pruning metrics (magnitude, gradient sensitivity, activation frequency) measure neuron-level importance, not feature-level coverage — so a polysemantic neuron encoding five weak features might outscore a monosemantic neuron encoding one critical but rarely-activated feature, even if losing that single feature catastrophically degrades a specific capability. The expert worry is therefore not about overall benchmark degradation (which is what most pruning papers report) but about silent capability loss: the model retains aggregate performance while quietly losing sparse, specialized features that only matter on tail-distribution inputs or safety-relevant edge cases.

Causal role in output is the property that should dominate the pruning safety decision, but it must be measured conditionally — not averaged over the training distribution. A feature that fires rarely but, when it does, is the decisive factor in the model's output (high causal effect on the logit difference for the relevant token) is maximally unsafe to prune. Anthropic's sparse autoencoder work on Claude and the earlier Toy Models of Superposition paper (Elman et al. / Bricken et al., 2022–2023) make this concrete: features in superposition are specifically those that are infrequent enough that the model can tolerate their interference costs — which means infrequency is actually a marker of superposition and thus a poor proxy for unimportance. Nanda et al.'s circuit-level work on indirect object identification shows that a handful of "name mover" heads carry nearly all the causal weight for that task, and ablating even one drops accuracy sharply; by activation magnitude alone, those heads are not especially prominent. The right operationalization is therefore something like conditional average treatment effect: what is the expected change in output quality on inputs where this feature is active, if you zero out the feature? Sun et al.'s Wanda pruning (2023) moves slightly in this direction by weighting magnitude by input activation norms, but still doesn't isolate feature-level causal effects — it remains a neuron-level heuristic. The expert concern is that building a truly safe pruning criterion requires causal scrubbing or activation patching at the feature level, which is computationally expensive and only recently tractable with sparse autoencoders.

The central new failure mode is reconstruction drift: when you prune a SAE feature and then reconstruct activations through the remaining features, the decoder vectors of surviving features shift their effective contribution because the pruned feature's variance must go somewhere — the SAE was trained assuming all features are present, so removing one breaks the implicit coverage assumptions baked into every other feature's decoder direction. This is qualitatively different from neuron pruning, where you remove a column from the weight matrix and the remaining columns are structurally unchanged. A second failure mode is feature boundary instability: SAE features are not perfectly orthogonal, and Anthropic's April 2024 scaling SAE work (Gao et al.) documents that at larger dictionary sizes, features fragment — one "concept" splits across multiple nearby features — meaning pruning what looks like a redundant near-duplicate feature may actually remove a necessary shard of a distributed representation. Third, SAE training itself introduces reconstruction error residuals (the "error term" that all current SAEs carry), and pruning based on SAE features implicitly assumes the SAE is a faithful enough map of the underlying computation; if it isn't, your pruning decisions are being made on a lossy proxy, and the errors compound when you retrain or fine-tune post-pruning. Muddy et al.'s work on SAE feature absorption (2024) adds a fourth concern: some features are "absorbed" by other features during SAE training in ways that aren't semantically transparent, so pruning the absorbing feature can silently kill the absorbed one with no obvious signal in the feature's own activation statistics. The deepest expert worry is that SAE features are defined relative to a frozen model, but pruning changes the model — there's no guarantee the SAE's feature decomposition remains valid after even modest weight removal.

There are two principled directions, but both carry significant costs. The first is co-training: jointly optimizing the base model and the SAE so that the sparse feature decomposition is a constraint on the model rather than a post-hoc analysis of it — this is essentially what Templeton et al. gesture at when discussing "features as the right unit of analysis," but nobody has demonstrated it at scale because the SAE loss and the LM loss interact destructively; the SAE pushes toward clean sparse representations while the LM loss pushes toward whatever weight configuration minimizes next-token prediction, and these are not naturally aligned. The second direction is iterative pruning with SAE retraining: prune a small fraction of weights, retrain the SAE on the new model, prune again — treating the SAE as a diagnostic that gets refreshed each round rather than a fixed map. This is principled but expensive; given that training a competitive SAE on a single layer of a medium-sized model already costs millions of tokens and significant compute (Gao et al. 2024 report dictionary sizes of up to 1M features), doing this iteratively across all layers and pruning rounds is currently intractable. A more radical departure is dictionary learning as a training objective from scratch — building sparsity into the model architecture directly, as in mixture-of-experts or the more aggressive sparse MLP proposals from Mistral and others, so that "features" are architectural units rather than emergent phenomena discovered post-hoc. The honest assessment is that the field doesn't yet have a satisfying solution: current SAE-based interpretability and current pruning methods were developed on orthogonal assumptions, and making them jointly stable likely requires rethinking what "a feature" means at the level of the training objective itself — closer to the neurosymbolic or modular network literature than to anything in mainstream transformer scaling.

The core capability loss would be combinatorial feature composition: dense superposition allows a single forward pass to implicitly compute exponentially many feature combinations by exploiting interference patterns across neurons, which Elhage et al.'s Toy Models paper formalizes — with n neurons you can represent O(n log n) or more features if you tolerate bounded interference. Architectural sparsity breaks this by forcing features into non-overlapping or weakly-overlapping slots, which hard-caps representational capacity at something much closer to O(n). Concretely, this matters most for analogical and relational reasoning: tasks like indirect object identification, multi-hop factual retrieval, and in-context learning likely depend on the model dynamically constructing transient feature combinations that exist nowhere as a stable circuit — they arise from superposition interacting across layers, not from any single monosemantic unit. Mixture-of-experts architectures, the closest production analog to enforced sparsity, illustrate the tradeoff empirically: Mixtral 8x7B routes tokens to 2 of 8 experts per layer, achieving strong efficiency, but independent analyses (Zyphra, EleutherAI, 2023–2024) show MoE models underperform dense models of equivalent active parameter count on tasks requiring fine-grained cross-domain composition, precisely where superposition's combinatorial expressivity matters. There's also a gradient flow cost that's underappreciated: in dense models, superposition means many weights receive gradient signal from many different features simultaneously, creating a rich implicit curriculum where learning one concept slightly adjusts the substrate for adjacent concepts. Enforced sparsity severs these gradient cross-talks, likely slowing learning on low-frequency concepts that would otherwise hitchhike on the dense feature interference structure — this is speculative but consistent with the known sample-efficiency gap between MoE and dense models at equal compute.

The detection problem is genuinely hard because standard weight-space analysis is the wrong instrument — you need activation-space probes run on inputs specifically designed to require the combination. The most tractable current method is causal scrubbing with compositional test sets: construct minimal pairs where the correct answer requires holding two features active simultaneously across layers, then measure the KL divergence between the original and pruned model's output distributions only on those inputs. Goldowsky-Dill et al.'s causal scrubbing paper (2023) provides the formal apparatus, but applying it to detect destroyed combinations requires knowing in advance what combinations to test — which is circular if you don't already know what the model was computing. A more discovery-oriented approach is activation pattern clustering across layers: run the pre- and post-pruning model on a large diverse corpus, record joint activation vectors at consecutive layers, and look for input clusters where the pruned model's layer-to-layer activation trajectories diverge from the original's even when final outputs match — this catches cases where the model reroutes through a degraded path that happens to produce the right answer on common inputs but will fail on distribution shift. Anthropic's sparse autoencoder work suggests a related diagnostic: if post-pruning you retrain an SAE on the pruned model and compare feature dictionaries, features that disappear or merge in the new SAE but were present before are candidates for destroyed combinations — though this is indirect and expensive. The deepest problem is that behavioral tests on standard benchmarks are nearly blind to this failure mode: a transient combination might be critical only for inputs at the intersection of two rare conditions, meaning you need either adversarially constructed evals or very large held-out sets with known compositional structure — neither of which exists systematically for most capability domains today.

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-1000)
response:
A purpose-built eval suite would need to measure conditional compositional accuracy: performance on inputs where the correct answer is only reachable by successfully binding two or more features that are individually rare, testing not just whether the model gets the answer right but whether the internal pathway used matches the expected compositional route — which requires activation-level instrumentation, not just output scoring. The suite would need at least three distinct probe types: conjunction stress tests (inputs requiring simultaneous activation of two low-frequency features, e.g. "a legal concept that applies only in maritime contexts involving minors"), cross-domain analogical chains (where step N's output must be encoded as a feature that feeds step N+1 in a different domain), and adversarial near-misses (inputs where one component of the required combination is present but the other is absent, to verify the model isn't pattern-matching on partial cues). What makes this harder than direct capability evals is the baseline problem: for direct loss, you know what the model should output and can score it; for compositional degradation, you need to verify that the model is using the right mechanism, not just producing the right token — a pruned model might answer a compositional question correctly via a shortcut that will fail on the next distributional shift, and output-level scoring cannot distinguish these. MATH and BIG-Bench compositional splits gesture at this but don't instrument internals; the RAVEL benchmark (Huang et al., 2024) is closer, isolating attribute-entity binding, but was designed for localization, not pruning stress-testing. Designing the evals is also harder because you must control for memorization: any compositional test item that appears near-literally in pretraining data collapses into direct recall, so the eval requires either synthetic data with verifiable novelty or careful n-gram deduplication against the training corpus — a methodological burden that standard capability evals don't face. The hardest part is the combinatorial coverage problem: the space of possible feature pairs is enormous, you can't enumerate it, and any finite eval suite will only sample a tiny fraction, meaning a model could pass all your compositional probes while silently losing combinations you didn't think to test.

The most promising internal signature is representational alignment under intervention: in intact compositional computation, if you patch the intermediate representation carrying feature A into a context requiring A+B composition, the downstream activations should shift predictably toward the A+B combination — whereas in fragile rerouting, the same patch produces erratic or attenuated downstream effects because the rerouted pathway doesn't have a clean slot for externally-injected feature signals. This is measurable via activation patching without any behavioral eval, and a systematic drop in patch effectiveness post-pruning is a mechanistic red flag even when outputs look correct. A second signature is attention entropy on compositional inputs: intact binding typically shows sharp, low-entropy attention patterns where specific heads reliably route feature A's representation to the position where feature B is being processed; rerouted computation tends to show higher, more diffuse attention entropy on those same heads because the model is spreading its bets across multiple weak pathways — Olsson et al.'s induction head work and subsequent circuit analyses consistently show that clean circuits have surprisingly low-entropy attention on their critical inputs. Third, singular value structure of intermediate residual stream states may distinguish the two regimes: intact composition tends to produce residual stream activations that lie in a low-dimensional subspace consistent with the expected feature combination, while rerouting produces activations with higher effective rank and less consistent directional structure across examples requiring the same composition — this is related to the "residual stream as communication channel" framing in Elhage et al. 2021. The honest caveat is that none of these signatures has been validated as a reliable discriminator in a pruning context specifically; they're motivated extrapolations from circuit-level interpretability findings, and a rigorous empirical test — comparing these internal metrics against ground-truth cases where rerouting is known to be fragile — hasn't been published. The field is close to being able to run this experiment given current SAE tooling, but the gap between "theoretically motivated signature" and "validated diagnostic" remains significant.
